packet_layer.unit: U1, PR 1: framing, acknowledgment, escapes, run-length decoding, hex, the interrupt byte and the caps, in sniff's own code under src/remote/, with unit rows natively and on the checked machine, red first
packet_layer.framing: `$` DATA `#` CC, CC the two hex digits of the sum of DATA's bytes modulo 256 (Overview). sniff sends lower-case digits and accepts either case. Numbers are hex with leading zeros suppressed (Overview); sniff sends them so and accepts leading zeros
packet_layer.acknowledgment: each packet is answered `+` (received) or `-` (resend), both ways (Overview, Packet Acknowledgment). A packet sniff receives with a wrong checksum gets `-`; a `-` from the stub makes sniff send the same packet again
packet_layer.no_ack: sniff sends QStartNoAckMode only when the qSupported reply holds `QStartNoAckMode+`; after the stub's `OK`, sniff acknowledges that reply with `+` and then neither sends nor expects acknowledgments for the rest of the connection; checksums are still sent and checked (Packet Acknowledgment; General Query Packets, QStartNoAckMode). MEASURED: QEMU 11.1.2 does not offer QStartNoAckMode (measured), so against QEMU sniff stays in acknowledgment mode; the no-ack rows run on the stand-in stub only
packet_layer.escape: binary data escapes `#`, `$` and `}` (and `*` in a stub's replies) as `}` then the byte XOR 0x20 (Overview). sniff decodes it in binary replies (qXfer's `m` and `l` data); the packets sniff sends carry no binary data in PR 1, so it never needs to escape
packet_layer.run_length: a reply may hold `C*N`: C repeated N-29 more times, N printable, never `#` or `$` (Overview). sniff decodes it in every reply and never sends it
packet_layer.interrupt: the single byte 0x03, outside any packet, while the target runs (Interrupts); a 0x03 inside a packet is data. sniff sends it on the user's interrupt and then waits for the stop reply
packet_layer.notifications: a `%` packet (a notification) is refused by name: notifications belong to non-stop mode, outside the closed list
packet_layer.standard_replies: an empty reply (`$#00`) means the packet is not supported; `E` and two hex digits is an error whose number the protocol does not define; `E.` and text is an error in words (Standard Replies). The `m` reply carries `E.text` only after `error-message` in qSupported (Packets, General Query Packets); sniff does not send `error-message`

caps.packet_size: the stub's `PacketSize=` from qSupported is the most data sniff sends in one packet (General Query Packets, PacketSize); sniff caps it at 16384; without the feature, the size is taken from the length of the `g` reply's data, as the manual says gdb guesses it. A reply's data is refused by name past 65536 bytes after decoding. Rows: each cap at its value and one past. MEASURED: QEMU answers PacketSize=20020 (131104 bytes), so sniff's own cap of 16384 is the one that applies
caps.retransmissions: a packet answered `-`, or not acknowledged in the reply time, is sent again at most 3 times; the fourth failure ends the command by name and leaves the connection as gdb would (gdb's words when a stub stops answering are not in the closed list and were not measured in U0, so sniff's words are its own and the row says so). Rows: 3 resends, then the fourth
caps.reply_time: 2 seconds for an acknowledgment and for a reply to a packet that does not resume the target, the default the manual gives for `set remotetimeout` (Remote Configuration); a resumption's stop reply has no time limit, and the interrupt is the way out (Interrupts). Rows: a reply at the limit and one past it, on a stand-in stub

packet_layer.stand_in_stub: U1's unit rows drive the packet layer against byte strings and against a small stand-in stub inside the unit test (sniff's own code, scripted replies over a socket pair), never against another implementation

client.unit: U2, PR 1: `target remote HOST:PORT`, `disconnect`, `detach`, `kill`, and the session commands over a remote target, as a third source behind src/session/source.lu's src_* reads (beside the live process and the core)
connect: `target remote HOST:PORT` and `target remote :PORT` (Connecting); TCP only in PR 1. sniff's refusals of the forms Connecting lists but sniff does not take (a serial device, `|` command, udp) are by name in sniff's words

after the TCP connect, in order: `qSupported` with sniff's features, QStartNoAckMode when offered, `?` for the stop that holds the target (Packets, `?`), the target description (Retrieving Descriptions), the thread list, and the registers of the stopped thread

sniff's qSupported features (General Query Packets): `swbreak+;hwbreak+;vContSupported+;xmlRegisters=i386`. Not `multiprocess`, so thread ids are plain (Packets, thread-id syntax) and `W`, `X` and `D` carry no pid; not `error-message`, not the event features

the description: `qXfer:features:read:target.xml:OFFSET,LENGTH`, then each `xi:include` annex the same way, reading `m` chunks until `l` (General Query Packets, qXfer read; Target Description Format, Inclusion)

MEASURED, what the pinned gdb sent to QEMU at connect, in order (measured): qSupported, vCont?, vMustReplyEmpty, Hgp0.0, qXfer:features:read of target.xml and of i386-64bit.xml in three 0x1000-byte chunks, qTStatus, ?, qfThreadInfo/qsThreadInfo, qAttached:1, Hc-1, qC, qOffsets, g, the thread list again, m of one byte at the pc, qSymbol::. sniff's own order is the one above it; qTStatus, qAttached, qOffsets, qSymbol and vMustReplyEmpty belong to features sniff does not have and are not sent
client.description: parsed as the Target Description Format's subset sniff needs: `<architecture>`, `<feature name=...>`, `<reg name= bitsize= regnum= type= group=>` with regnum's default one more than the previous register's and 0 first, and `<xi:include href=...>`. Types: the predefined ones by name (Predefined Target Types) and `<vector>`, `<union>`, `<flags>` and `<struct>` read for their sizes and names. sniff requires `org.gnu.gdb.i386.core` with rax-r15, rip, eflags, cs, ss, ds, es, fs, gs, st0-st7 and fctrl-fop, takes `org.gnu.gdb.i386.sse` when present (i386 Features), and shows other features' registers as the description names them (Standard Target Features). A description that lacks a required register is refused by name. MEASURED: QEMU's target.xml names the architecture i386:x86-64 and includes one further annex, which holds a single feature, org.gnu.gdb.i386.core, with 66 registers: the general registers and rip, eflags and the segment selectors, QEMU's own segment bases, control registers and efer, the x87 registers, xmm0-xmm15 and mxcsr. There is no org.gnu.gdb.i386.sse feature, so sniff takes the SSE registers from whichever feature names them. The g reply is 608 bytes.
client.registers: `g` gives every register in regnum order, two hex digits a byte in target order (little-endian), `x`s for a register the stub cannot read (Packets, g); `p N` reads one register (regnum in hex). `P N=R` writes one (Packets). sniff reads with `g` and falls back to `p` when `g`'s reply is short of a register
client.memory: `m ADDR,LEN` reads LEN bytes as hex pairs, possibly fewer (Packets, m); `M ADDR,LEN:XX` writes, `OK` or an error (Packets, M). A read past the packet size is split. A short or error reply is gdb's `Cannot access memory at address 0x...`
client.breakpoints: `Z0,ADDR,KIND` and `z0,...` for a software breakpoint, `Z1` for a hardware one, `Z2`, `Z3` and `Z4` for write, read and access watchpoints (Packets, z and Z). KIND for x86: the manual leaves it to the architecture (Packets, Z0) and its x86 node is not in the list (Architecture-Specific Protocol Details names only ARM and MIPS); MEASURED: the pinned gdb sends KIND 1 for Z0 and Z1 on x86-64 (measured), the length of int3, and sniff sends 1; Z2 carries the watched length (8 for an 8-byte word). An empty reply means the type is not supported; an error means the stub could not insert it. MEASURED (measured): under KVM QEMU puts a software breakpoint into guest memory, so an m of its address reads 0xcc; under TCG the same read gives the original byte. gdb's transcripts were equal because gdb shows its own breakpoints' original bytes; sniff does the same, from the byte it read before the Z0, so x, the disassembly and the CFI reads never depend on the accelerator. Its own row, remote-kernel-break-shadow, reads a breakpoint's address with x under KVM and under TCG and holds both to the original byte
client.resume: `vCont?` once; then `vCont;c` and `vCont;s:TID` when listed, else `c` and `s` (Packets, vCont and vCont?). The stop reply is waited for with no time limit
client.stop_replies: `T AA n:r;...` with register values, `thread:TID`, `core:N`, and one stop reason of `watch:ADDR`, `rwatch:ADDR`, `awatch:ADDR`, `swbreak:` or `hwbreak:`; unknown n:r pairs ignored; `S AA`; `W AA` exit; `X AA` killed by a signal; `O XX` console output printed as it comes (Stop Reply Packets). Register values in a T reply are taken in place of the `g` read for those registers
client.signals: the manual defines only `05`, the trap signal (Stop Reply Packets); it gives every other number's meaning to gdb's source, which stays closed, include/gdb/signals.h included. So every number sniff names is a binary observation paired with the name printed in the same run: for the client, QEMU's stop reply in the pinned gdb's packet log beside the signal name gdb printed (observed in the Linux measurement's session A, under KVM and TCG: `T02thread:p01.01;` after the 0x03, printed `Program received signal SIGINT, Interrupt.`; `T05core:01;` at a reconnect, printed `Program received signal SIGTRAP, Trace/breakpoint trap.`; 05 at every breakpoint and step. So PR 1's table holds 02 SIGINT and 05 SIGTRAP, each with that measurement as its source). sniff's table of protocol numbers holds only observed numbers and records the measurement that observed each; a number never observed prints as an unknown signal, by name. The stub's numbers (PR 2) come from gdbserver's T reply for a fixture raising each of signals 1 to 31
client.threads: `qfThreadInfo` then `qsThreadInfo` until `l` (General Query Packets); `qC` for the current thread; `Hg TID` before `g`, `p`, `m` of another thread (Packets, H). At one processor QEMU names one thread; the mechanism is built here for U4. MEASURED by the same run: with no multiprocess offered, qfThreadInfo answers `m01` and qC `QC01` (plain thread ids), qSupported's reply is unchanged, and `?` still answers `T05core:01;`
client.end: `detach` sends `D` and closes after `OK` (Packets, D; Connecting, detach); `disconnect` closes the socket and sends nothing, leaving the target stopped (Connecting, disconnect); `kill` sends `k` and expects no reply, a closed connection counting as success (Packets, k). MEASURED (measured): gdb, having offered multiprocess, sent `D;1` and `vKill;1`, each answered OK, and QEMU ended after vKill (`QEMU: Terminated via GDBstub`); `disconnect` sent nothing. sniff offers no multiprocess and sends `D` and `k`. MEASURED by sniff's first development run (2026-11-23 08:10Z, sniff's packet layer against the Mac's pinned QEMU, frozen at reset): `k` is acknowledged with `+`, the connection closes, and QEMU ends (`QEMU: Terminated via GDBstub`) within 0.2 s, so `k` serves and vKill is not needed
client.session: `break` by function, `file:line` and `*ADDR`, from the kernel ELF's DWARF; `hbreak`; `watch`; `continue`; `stepi`, `step`, `next` and `finish` built on `s` and breakpoints as for a live process; `bt` by the CFI in .debug_frame with the stack read by `m`; `info registers` and `info all-registers` from the description; `x`; `print`; `info locals`; `info threads`; the interrupt
client.description_text: the annex QEMU sends is a third party's copyrighted file (it carries the Free Software Foundation's notice: QEMU's copy of a file from gdb's features directory). sniff parses it off the wire at run time and never carries it: no copy of it, in whole or in part, is in this repository, in fixtures, goldens, recorded wire logs or test inputs. A unit row that needs a description uses one written here from the Target Description Format and i386 Features nodes; a row about QEMU's own description names it by sha256 only. sniff-server's description (PR 2) is written from the i386 Features node alone

session C: `detach` and `kill` with no target: `The program is not being run.`; `disconnect`: ``You can't do that when your target is `exec'``; `target remote 127.0.0.1:1` and `:70000`: `could not connect: Connection refused.`; an unresolvable name: `NAME:PORT: cannot resolve name: Temporary failure in name resolution`; `127.0.0.1:`: `Missing port on hostname '127.0.0.1:'`; no address: the three-line `To open a remote debug connection, you need to specify what` paragraph; `info threads`: `No threads.`

kernel_symbols.breakpoints: kmain (0xffffffff80117600, kmain_console.lu:553), reached on every boot; its first callee identity.mark_entry (0xffffffff800bc623); kmain_console.lu:560, `bootmark.start(bootlog.start())`
kernel_symbols.globals: the kernel's DWARF names only two addressed variables, both in the Rust runtime's compile unit: LIVE_REGION_BYTES (0xffffffff806524c0, core::sync::atomic::Atomic<usize>) and AMBIENT_REGION (0xffffffff806524b8). wolf's own globals are in the symbol table only (for example `_Wbootmark.blind.sbef3515187e1839`, a bss byte). So `print` of a kernel global is measured three ways (the Rust value, the symbol with no type, and the symbol cast to a type) and the rows take what sniff's printer already handles; a Rust-language value is out of PR 1's scope if gdb prints it in Rust's syntax. MEASURED: from a wolf frame gdb does not see LIVE_REGION_BYTES at all, and the symbol-only global needs a cast; so remote-kernel-print is the cast form, `print (unsigned char) '_Wbootmark.blind.sbef3515187e1839'`, which sniff's printer must take (a C cast of a symbol without debug information)

where.mac_scored: predicted in PR 1; moved to a follow-up PR. Building the session showed that sniff chooses its architecture at compile time (paired host-conditional functions in the arch layer and the session), so sniff built for the arm64 Mac has no x86-64 register map, CFI columns or call detection and cannot debug the x86-64 kernel. PR 1 is the Linux session over a remote target, where host and target are both x86-64, and its Mac rows are skipped by name with that reason. The follow-up makes the arch tables functions of an arch id with the session carrying its target's arch, shows every existing row byte-identical before and after on both hosts, adds units for both tables on both hosts red first, then the Mac kernel rows
where.hosted_linux_scored: predicted: the image, under TCG. Decided before the rows: hosted Linux skips the kernel rows by name, as it skips the PAX legs, because no kernel image is on that host (PAX's console image is built only on the record host). The skip names that reason in one line, and the hosted log's skip count is a held number, so a row that stops running elsewhere shows. The record host runs the kernel rows under KVM and, as its own step, under TCG, so TCG's answers are on record by name. A pinned image fetched by digest is a follow-up once a package host serves artifacts by digest
where.linux_tcg: the image under TCG on the record host, as its own step of the record's manifest

signal_numbers.decision: every number sniff names is a binary observation paired with the name printed in the same run: for the client, QEMU's stop reply beside gdb's printed name; for the stub (PR 2), gdbserver's T reply for a fixture raising each of signals 1 to 31. The table records which measurement observed each number, and an unobserved number prints as unknown by name. gdb's source stays closed, signals.h included. The stub's plant then goes red at a row whose host and protocol numbers differ, named from that measurement, because Linux's SIGTRAP is 5 and the protocol's trap is 05
